questions.q: Why is benchmark contamination a threat to a reported reasoning improvement?
options: It makes the model run slower at inference time
If benchmark problems or close variants leaked into training data, a high score can reflect memorization of that specific problem set rather than a generalizable reasoning improvement
It only affects code benchmarks, never math benchmarks
It has no effect on reported scores
questions.explain: Contaminated benchmarks can inflate scores through memorization, which is why checking for leaked or near-duplicate problems in training data matters before trusting a score.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say comparing a baseline model at n_samples=1 against a new model at n_samples=32 with search is a meaningless comparison?
options: Because n_samples has no effect on accuracy

Because lesson 58 showed that more sampling and search improve scores on a fixed policy with zero training change, so the score gap could come entirely from the mismatched inference budget rather than from anything learned during training
Because the two models must always use the same verifier
Because 32 samples is always worse than 1 sample
questions.explain: Test-time compute alone can raise scores without any change to the policy, so an inference-budget mismatch between two evaluated systems makes the comparison uninformative about training improvements.

questions.q: What does pass@1 measure, and why does the lesson recommend reporting it for training comparisons?
options: The percentage of users who pass a certification exam
Accuracy from a single sample per problem, which isolates what actually changed in the trained policy itself, separate from any test-time search or sampling boost
The number of passes a verifier makes over the code before timing out
The pass rate when using 32 samples and PRM-guided search
questions.explain: pass@1 reflects single-shot policy quality, uncontaminated by the additional gains that come purely from spending more inference-time compute.

questions.q: What does a trace faithfulness audit check that a standard benchmark score cannot?
options: Whether the model's final answer is formatted correctly
Whether the reasoning displayed in a trace actually drove the final answer, rather than the model landing on a correct answer through some other, undisplayed process (unfaithful chain-of-thought)
Whether the model uses a GPU or a CPU
Whether the benchmark itself is contaminated
questions.explain: A benchmark score only checks the final answer; a faithfulness audit (e.g. truncating or corrupting a step to see if the answer changes appropriately) checks whether the stated reasoning was actually necessary and causal.

questions.q: What combination does this lesson recommend as the strongest practical standard for evaluating a reasoning improvement?
options: A single leaderboard score is sufficient on its own
Evaluating on genuinely fresh, uncontaminated problems, holding inference-time compute fixed while reporting pass@1, and spot-checking a sample of traces for faithfulness
Only checking benchmark contamination, with no other checks needed
Only using best-of-n search results, ignoring pass@1 entirely
questions.explain: The lesson combines three defenses — freshness, compute-matched pass@1 comparison, and faithfulness spot-checks — as a meaningfully stronger standard than any single aggregate benchmark number.
